```{r}
#| label: helpers

# ---- Voting plot used on several slides ------------------------------------
# Scatter of the binary outcome against statusquo. With densities = TRUE, adds a
# density curve for each outcome group. Add smoothers/annotations after calling.
vote_plot <- function(d, densities = TRUE, from = NULL, to = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(statusquo, vote, col = voteYN)) + 
    geom_point() + 
    scale_color_manual(values = c(my_blue, my_purple)) +
    guides(color = "none") + 
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Vote", labels = c("No", "Yes"), 
                       breaks = c(0, 1), limits = c(-.1, 1.1)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
  
  if (densities) {
    dens <- function(v) {
      dd <- if (is.null(from)) density(v) else density(v, from = from, to = to)
      data.frame(x = dd$x, y = dd$y)
    }
    d0 <- dens(d$statusquo[d$vote == 0])
    d1 <- dens(d$statusquo[d$vote == 1])
    p <- p + 
      geom_path(data = d0, aes(x, y * .5), col = my_blue, linewidth = 1, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
      geom_path(data = d1, aes(x, 1 - y * .5), col = my_purple, linewidth = 1, inherit.aes = FALSE)
  }
  p
}

# ---- Ellipse outline (replaces tikz \draw ... ellipse) ----------------------
ellipse_df <- function(x0, y0, a, b, n = 100) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length = n)
  data.frame(x = x0 + a * cos(t), y = y0 + b * sin(t))
}

# ---- Formatting helpers for inline numbers ---------------------------------
f   <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f")            # fixed decimals
nz  <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", f(x, d))                # drop leading zero
pm  <- function(x, d = 2) if (x < 0) paste("-", f(abs(x), d)) else paste("+", f(x, d))
fp  <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))         # APA p-value
chg <- function(x) if (x < 0) "decrease" else "increase"
```

## Types of Linear Models

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

**General Linear Model**

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p$$

- ANOVA, $t$-tests, linear regression are special cases

- Assumes a linear relationship between the DV and (a linear combination of) predictor(s)

**General**[**ized**]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} **Linear Model**

$$f(\hat{y}) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p$$

- $f$ is a nonlinear function

- Assumes a **nonlinear** relationship between the DV and (a linear combination of) predictor(s)

:::

## Transformation

General Linear Model with Transformed Criterion:

$$\widehat{f(y)} = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p$$

$$y = f^{-1}(b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p + e)$$

- Changes the interpretation of the criterion
- Transformation must [both]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} improve linearity and achieve homogeneity of variance
- Transformation may not be defined for all $y$ values (e.g., $\ln(0) = -\infty$)


## Generalization

Generalized Linear Model:

$$f(\hat{y}) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p$$

$$y = f^{-1}(b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p) + e$$

- Transforms the **predicted value** $\hat{y}$
- "Normalizes" the residuals $e$
- Changes the interpretation of the **coefficients**




## Other Types of $y$'s

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em;"}

Nearly all methods we've learned so far have assumed a continuous, normally distributed outcome variable and/or residuals

Often, this is implausible:

- Categorical outcome

- Count data

- Symptom inventory with many zeros

For today, let's consider a binary outcome variable

- Want to model/predict the **probability** of observing one outcome instead of the other
  
- Probability can be thought of as the average of a binary variable (categories coded 0 or 1)

:::

## General Linear Model

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em;"}

The multiple regression model we have learned so far is also known as ordinary least squares (OLS) regression (after the method used to obtain estimated coefficients)

Three characteristics of OLS regression:

1. Linear in coefficients (linear in parameters)

    - Predicted outcome is a linear combination of predictors, where weights are regression coefficients

2. Distribution of residuals:
  
    - Assume normally distributed

    - Assume homoscedasticity

3. Score of predicted outcome ($\hat{y}$)

    - $\hat{y}$ has the same units as the observed outcome $y$
    
:::

## Generalized Linear Model

**General**[**ized**]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} **linear models (GLMs)** are a broad class of regression models that allows for nonlinear relationships between predictors and the criterion

- Useful for discrete outcomes, counts

OLS regression is a special case of a GLM

GLMs do not necessarily assume a continuous outcome, normally distributed residuals, or homoscedasticity

**Logistic regression** is one of the most popular GLMs for predicting **probabilities** of binary categorical outcomes.

## Example: Voting Behavior

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

In 1973, Augusto Pinochet took power in Chile after a (US-backed) coup d'état, after which the country was ruled by a military dictatorship. In 1988, a referendum was taken to a public vote with options "Yes" - elect Pinochet to hold office for another 8 years, or "No" - hold presidential and parliamentary elections. The "No" vote won, and Chile has been ruled democratically since 1990.

The data is from a national survey conducted about 5 months before the referendum.

The dataset includes demographic information and voting intentions from 2700 Chileans, including:

- `vote`: "Y" yes (for Pinochet), "N" no (against Pinochet), "A" abstain, "U" undecided

- `statusquo`: Standardized measure of support for the status quo (higher values indicate greater support)

- `education`: "P" primary school, "S" secondary school, "PS" post-secondary school

Goal: predict voting intentions from demographics

:::

## Voting Data

For this analysis, we will only include survey participants who responded "Yes" or "No". We will also omit the small number of cases with missing data on the `vote`, `education`, or `statusquo` variables. Now there are 1747 observations

```{r}
options(width = 75)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true

data(Chile, package = "carData")
Chile <- Chile %>%
  filter(!is.na(education) & !is.na(statusquo) & 
           vote %in% c("Y", "N")) %>%
  mutate(voteYN = factor(vote),
         vote = as.numeric(vote == "Y")) %>%
  as_tibble
Chile
```

:::

## Probability $\rightarrow$ Normality


::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

Probabilities are distributed between 0 and 1. The **uniform** probability distribution is a distribution such that all values between 0 and 1 are equally likely. 

```{r}
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-height: 4

unif <- data.frame(P = seq(0, 1, by = .01))

ggplot(unif, aes(x = P)) + 
  geom_segment(x = 0, xend = 1, y = 1, yend = 1) + 
  geom_segment(x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 1) + 
  geom_segment(x = 1, xend = 1, y = 0, yend = 1) + 
  xlim(c(-0.25, 1.25)) + 
  ylim(c(0, 1.5)) + 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
```

**Problem:** Probability is **double bounded**. How can we map probability onto something like a normal distribution?


::: 

## Probability $\rightarrow$ Odds

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

Step 1: Convert probability to  $odds = \frac{P}{1-P}$

```{r}
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-height: 4

ggplot(unif, aes(x = P/(1-P))) + geom_density() + xlim(c(0, 10)) + 
  ylab(NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
```

Odds are only **single** bounded. How can we now get odds to be **unbounded**?

::: 

## Odds $\rightarrow$ Log Odds

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

Step 2: Take the **log** (when we say log we usually will mean natural log by default)

```{r}
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-height: 4

ggplot(unif, aes(x = log(P/(1-P)))) + geom_density() + xlim(c(-10, 10)) + 
  ylab(NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
```

$ln(1) = 0$. Taking the log makes anything between 0 and 1 negative, and anything greater than 1 positive (anything below 0 is undefined)

:::

## Logit Function




We can now estimate our model in log odds, aka **logit** units, as 

$$ln\left(\frac{P}{1-P}\right) = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \cdots + b_p x_p$$

The inverse of the **logit** function is known as the **logistic** function, and allows us to write the model in probability units instead of logit units.

## Logistic Function

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="68%"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

The **logistic** function, also known as the **inverse logit** function of a quantity $w$ is:

$$\text{logit}^{-1}(w) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-w)} = \frac{\exp(w)}{1 + \exp(w)}$$

$\text{logit}^{-1}(w)$ is a probability $P$, so

$$\begin{aligned}
  P & = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-w)} \\ 
  \exp(-w) & = \frac{1}{P} - 1 \\
  w & = \ln\left(\frac{P}{1-P}\right)
\end{aligned}$$

- $w$ is the log odds of success 
- "success" is category coded "1"
- "failure" is category coded "0"
- In statistics, you can usually safely assume the *natural* log $\ln()$

:::

::::

:::: {.column width="32%"}

::: {style="color: #4DAF4A; text-align: center; border: 3px solid #4DAF4A; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.6em; margin-top: 3em;"}

$\exp()$ and $\ln()$ are inverse functions

$-\ln(x) = \ln\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$

:::

::::

:::::

:::

## Our Example

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

In the voting example, we may use the following model:

$$P(\mathsf{yes}) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(b_0 + b_1\mathsf{statusquo}))}$$

$$\ln\left(\frac{P(\mathsf{yes})}{1 - P(\mathsf{yes})}\right) = b_0 + b_1\mathsf{statusquo}$$

- $b_0$: "intercept", the log odds of voting "yes" if status quo = 0
  
- $b_1$: "slope", the increase in log odds associated with a one-unit (1SD) increase in status quo

In general:

- Lower $b_0$ indicates a lower average probability of voting "yes" 

- Higher $b_1$ indicates a steeper slope, greater separation between categories

::: 

## Logistic Function



```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.5

x <- seq(-3, 3, length = 100)
curves <- data.frame(
  x = rep(x, 3), 
  y = c(1 / (1 + exp(-x)), 1 / (1 + exp(-2 * x + 1)), 1 / (1 + exp(-1 - x))),
  gp = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 100)
)

# Replaces the tikz node labels
ggplot(curves, aes(x, y, group = gp, col = gp)) + 
  geom_path(linewidth = 3) + 
  annotate("richtext", x = 1.6, y = .62, col = my_blue, size = 8, fill = NA, label.color = NA,
           label = "<b>b<sub>0</sub> = 0, b<sub>1</sub> = 1</b>") +
  annotate("richtext", x = 1.2, y = .33, col = my_green, size = 8, fill = NA, label.color = NA,
           label = "<b>b<sub>0</sub> = −1, b<sub>1</sub> = 2</b>") +
  annotate("richtext", x = -1.8, y = .82, col = my_purple, size = 8, fill = NA, label.color = NA,
           label = "<b>b<sub>0</sub> = 1, b<sub>1</sub> = 1</b>") +
  labs(y = "Probability") + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c(my_blue, my_green, my_purple)) + 
  guides(color = "none") + 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
```

## Single Predictor

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Logistic regression model with one predictor ($x_1$):

$$\hat{P} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(b_0 + b_1x_1))} = \frac{\exp(b_0 + b_1x_1)}{1 + \exp(b_0 + b_1x_1)}$$

- $\hat{P}$: predicted probability of the outcome $y = 1$ ($\hat{P}$ ranges from 0 to 1)

- A plot of $\hat{P}$ as a function of $x_1$ yields a logistic (S-shaped) curve

NOTICE: no residual term in this equation!

- Reason: observed outcome $y$ is binary (categories coded "0" and "1")

- Mean of $y$ = $\hat{P}$

- Variance of $y$ = $\hat{P} \times (1 - \hat{P})$

- Mean and variance of a binary variable are dependent

::: 

## Alternative Form


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

The logistic regression model can also be expressed as follows:

$$\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}} = \exp(b_0 + b_1x_1)$$

- $\exp(w) = e^w = 2.718^w$

- $\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}} =$ odds that $y = 1$

Odds ranges from 0 to $+\infty$

- When $\hat{P} = .5$, odds = 1

- When $\hat{P} > .5$, odds > 1

- When $\hat{P} < .5$, 0 < odds < 1

:::

## Another Alt Form

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em;"}

Yet another expression of the logistic regression model:

$$\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1$$

- $\ln()$: natural logarithmic function

- $\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) =$ logit
  
- The **logit** is the function of $\hat{P}$ that is linearly related to $x_1$
:::

## Logistic Regression in `R`

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Logistic regression models fit using the `glm()` function built into `R`

- Same formula notation as multiple linear regression

- Must add argument "`family = binomial`" to indicate logistic regression (instead of another GLM)

- Unlike linear regression, which uses ordinary least squares (OLS), `glm()` estimates the coefficients by **maximum likelihood**: an iterative procedure that finds the coefficient values that make the observed data most likely

```{r}
#| echo: true

glm1 <- glm(vote ~ statusquo, Chile, family = binomial)
coef(glm1)
```

```{r}
# Values used in the text of the following slides
cf1 <- summary(glm1)$coefficients
b0  <- cf1["(Intercept)", "Estimate"];  se0 <- cf1["(Intercept)", "Std. Error"]
b1  <- cf1["statusquo", "Estimate"];    se1 <- cf1["statusquo", "Std. Error"]
b0r <- round(b0, 2); b1r <- round(b1, 2)      # rounded values shown on slides
P_at    <- function(x) plogis(b0r + b1r * x)  # predicted probability
odds_at <- function(x) exp(b0r + b1r * x)     # predicted odds
ci0 <- b0 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(.975) * se0
ci1 <- b1 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(.975) * se1
```

These coefficients imply the following fitted equation: 

$$\hat{P}(\mathsf{vote\ yes}) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(`r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)`\times\mathsf{statusquo}))}$$

:::

## Intercept Interpretation

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

How to interpret the estimated regression coefficients?

$$\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1 = `r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)` \times \mathsf{statusquo}$$

- $b_0 = `r nz(b0r)`$: estimated intercept
    - logit when statusquo = 0 (average support for the status quo)
    - When statusquo = 0, $P(\mathsf{yes}) = \frac{1}{1+\exp(-(`r nz(b0r)`))} = `r nz(P_at(0))`$
    - May not have a meaningful interpretation if 0 never occurs in data


:::

## Slope Interpretation

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

How to interpret the estimated regression coefficients?

$$\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1 = `r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)` \times \mathsf{statusquo}$$

- $b_1 = `r f(b1r)`$
    - Change in logit for a one-unit (approx. 1 SD) increase in statusquo
    - How this affects predicted probability depends on the starting value:



$$\begin{aligned}
  P(\mathsf{yes} \vert -2) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(`r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)`\times -2))} & = `r nz(P_at(-2), 4)` \\
  P(\mathsf{yes} \vert -1) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(`r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)`\times -1))} & = `r nz(P_at(-1), 3)` \\
  P(\mathsf{yes} \vert 0) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(`r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)`\times 0))} & = `r nz(P_at(0), 3)`
\end{aligned}$$



:::

## Odds Intercept

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

How to interpret the estimated regression coefficients?

$$\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1 = `r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)` \times \mathsf{statusquo}$$

- $\exp(b_0) = \exp(`r nz(b0r)`) = `r f(exp(b0r))`$: estimated intercept in **odds**
    - when statusquo = 0 (average support for the status quo), a vote of yes is `r f(exp(b0r))` times as likely as no
    - When statusquo = 0, $P(\mathsf{yes}) = \frac{`r f(exp(b0r))`}{1+`r f(exp(b0r))`} = `r nz(P_at(0))`$
    - May not have a meaningful interpretation if 0 never occurs in data




:::


## Odds Slope

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

How to interpret the estimated regression coefficients?

$$\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1 = `r nz(b0r)` `r pm(b1r)` \times \mathsf{statusquo}$$

- $\exp(b_1) = \exp(`r f(b1r)`) = `r f(exp(b1r))`$
    - For one unit increase in statusquo, odds of yes (vs no) becomes `r f(exp(b1r))` times as large



$$\begin{aligned}
  \frac{P(\mathsf{yes} \vert -2)}{P(\mathsf{no} \vert -2)} &= \frac{`r nz(P_at(-2), 4)`}{1 - `r nz(P_at(-2), 4)`} = `r nz(odds_at(-2), 4)` \\
  \frac{P(\mathsf{yes} \vert -1)}{P(\mathsf{no} \vert -1)} &= \frac{`r nz(P_at(-1), 3)`}{1 - `r nz(P_at(-1), 3)`} = `r f(exp(b1r))`(`r nz(odds_at(-2), 4)`) = `r nz(odds_at(-1), 3)` \\
  \frac{P(\mathsf{yes} \vert 0)}{P(\mathsf{no} \vert 0)} &= \frac{`r nz(P_at(0), 3)`}{1 - `r nz(P_at(0), 3)`} = `r f(exp(b1r))`(`r nz(odds_at(-1), 3)`) = `r f(odds_at(0))`
\end{aligned}$$


:::

## Classification Accuracy

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

From the fitted model, we can calculate predicted probabilities for each observation

```{r}
#| echo: true

fitted1 <- fitted(glm1)
class1 <- ifelse(fitted1 > .5, 
                 "pred_yes", "pred_no")
table(class1, Chile$voteYN)
```

```{r}
tab1 <- table(class1, Chile$voteYN)
cor1 <- c(tab1["pred_no", "N"], tab1["pred_yes", "Y"])
acc1 <- sum(cor1) / sum(tab1)
```

$\frac{`r cor1[1]` + `r cor1[2]`}{`r sum(tab1)`} = `r f(100 * acc1)`\%$ of votes correctly classified using only status quo support as a predictor

Other considerations

- Is .5 the right cutoff? 
    - What if one category is much less likely than the other?
- This is classifying on the same sample as the one the model was estimated on
    - Cross validation?

:::

## Confidence Intervals

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

`glm` output gives each estimated regression coefficient and its standard error

- $z$-test assumes that sampling distributions of coefficients are normally distributed 

```{r}
#| echo: true

summary(glm1)$coefficients
```

Confidence interval for coefficient $j$:

$$b_j \pm z_{\alpha/2} s_{b_j}$$

Example:

$$\begin{aligned}
  95\%\ \text{CI}(b_0) & = `r f(b0)` \pm 1.96 \times `r nz(se0, 3)` = \boldsymbol{[`r nz(ci0[1], 3)`,\ `r nz(ci0[2], 3)`]} \\
  95\%\ \text{CI}(b_1) & = `r f(b1)` \pm 1.96 \times `r nz(se1, 3)` = \boldsymbol{[`r f(ci1[1])`,\ `r f(ci1[2])`]}
\end{aligned}$$

:::

## Model Comparison

::: {style="font-size: 0.67em;"}

For ordinary linear regression, we used $t$-tests to evaluate the significance of each predictor in the regression equation

For GLMs, we instead compare the fit of models that differ by only that predictor:

$$\begin{aligned}
  \text{Null Model} &: \ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 \\
  \text{Model 1} &: \ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
  \chi^2(\text{dif}) & = {\color{#FF7F00}{-2\times \text{logLikelihood}(\text{Null Model})}} - \left({\color{#FF7F00}{-2\times  \text{logLikelihood}(\text{Model 1})}}\right) \\ 
  & = \text{Deviance}(\text{Null Model}) - \text{Deviance}(\text{Model 1})
\end{aligned}$$

Then, $\chi^2(\text{dif}) \sim \chi^2(df)$, where $df$ equals the difference in the number of estimated parameters between Model 1 and the Null Model



- [**Null Model:** all predicted probabilities are the same]{style="color: #377EB8;"}

- [$-2\times$ log likelihood is evaluated at the maximum likelihood parameter estimates]{style="color: #FF7F00;"}

- [**Deviance** $= -2 \times$ log likelihood]{style="color: #4DAF4A;"}

:::

## Model Comparison in `R`

The `anova()` function (confusingly) is often used for model comparison

- Here, we compare model with intercept only (Null Model) to a model with both slope and intercept for `statusquo`

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true

anova(glm1, test = "LRT")
```

:::

```{r}
a1 <- anova(glm1, test = "LRT")
dev_null <- a1$`Resid. Dev`[1]
dev_1    <- a1$`Resid. Dev`[2]
chi1     <- a1$Deviance[2]
p1       <- a1$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
```

[`test = "LRT"` requests a "Likelihood Ratio Test"]{style="color: #FF7F00;"}

::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="color: #4DAF4A; border: 3px solid #4DAF4A; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.6em; font-size: 0.85em;"}

Null Model Deviance: `r f(dev_null)`  
Model 1 Deviance: `r f(dev_1)`  
$\chi^2(\text{dif}, 1) = `r f(chi1)`, p `r fp(p1)`$

Interpretation: Model 1 fits `r if (p1 < .05) "significantly better than" else "no better than"` the Null Model

:::

::::

:::::

## Adding Predictors

General logistic regression model:

$$\begin{aligned}
  \hat{P} & = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p))} \\ \\
  & = \frac{\exp(b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p)}{1 + \exp(b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p)}
\end{aligned}$$

- $p$ predictors 

- $\hat{P}$: predicted probability of the outcome $y = 1$ ($\hat{P}$ ranges from 0 to 1)
  
- Notice the linear combination of predictors: $b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_px_p$

## Predictor Interpretations

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

Interpreting parameters with 2 predictors:

$$\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2$$

$b_0$: estimated intercept

- logit when both $x_1 =0$ and $x_2 = 0$

$b_1$: estimated regression slope of $x_1$ on logit holding $x_2$ constant

- change of logit when $x_1$ increases by 1 unit, holding $x_2$ constant

$b_2$: estimated regression slope of $x_2$ on logit holding $x_1$ constant

- change of logit when $x_2$ increases by 1 unit, holding $x_1$ constant

:::

## Odds Interpretations

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

Interpreting parameters with 2 predictors:

$$\ln\left(\frac{\hat{P}}{1 - \hat{P}}\right) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2$$

$\exp(b_0)$: estimated intercept

- odds when both $x_1 =0$ and $x_2 = 0$

$\exp(b_1)$: factor by which odds change for one unit increase of $x_1$  holding $x_2$ constant

$\exp(b_2)$: factor by which odds change for one unit increase of $x_2$  holding $x_1$ constant

:::

## Multiple Predictors in `R` {.scrollable}

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

Let's add `education` to the model. Remember that `education` is a factor variable with 3 categories - `R` will represent this with 2 dummy variables

```{r}
#| echo: true

glm2 <- glm(vote ~ statusquo + education, Chile, family = binomial)
summary(glm2)$coefficients
```

```{r}
cf2 <- summary(glm2)$coefficients
bb  <- cf2[, "Estimate"]; ss <- cf2[, "Std. Error"]   # order: Intercept, statusquo, PS, S
lo2 <- bb - qnorm(.975) * ss; hi2 <- bb + qnorm(.975) * ss
```

We can see that "S" (secondary) and "PS" (post-secondary) each have their own coefficient - that means that "P" (primary) is the reference level

- $b_0 = `r nz(bb[1], 3)`$: logit for someone with a primary school education and the average support for the status quo

- $b_1 = `r f(bb[2])`$: change of logit when `statusquo` increases by 1 unit (1 SD), holding `education` constant

- $b_2 = `r f(bb[3])`$: `r chg(bb[3])` in logit (log odds) of voting "yes" for someone with a post-secondary education (vs. a primary school education), holding support for the status quo constant

- $b_3 = `r f(bb[4])`$: `r chg(bb[4])` in logit (log odds) of voting "yes" for someone with a secondary education (vs. a primary school education), holding support for the status quo constant

:::

## Odds Interpretations {.scrollable}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Odds interpretation of the same model:

```{r}
summary(glm2)$coefficients
```

- $\exp(b_0) = \exp(`r nz(bb[1], 3)`) = `r f(exp(bb[1]))`$: odds of yes vote (vs no) for someone with a primary school education and the average support for the status quo

- $\exp(b_1) = `r f(exp(bb[2]))`$: factor by which odds of yes vote (vs no) changes for one unit increase in statusquo holding education constant

- $\exp(b_2) = `r f(exp(bb[3]))`$: factor by which odds of yes vote (vs no) changes for someone with post-secondary education (vs a primary school education) holding statusquo constant

- $\exp(b_3) = `r f(exp(bb[4]))`$: factor by which odds of yes vote (vs no) changes for someone with secondary education (vs a primary school education) holding statusquo constant

:::

## Confidence Intervals

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{r}
summary(glm2)$coefficients
```

Confidence interval for (population) $b_j$:

$$b_j \pm z_{\alpha/2}\times s_{b_j}$$

- 95% CI for $b_0: `r nz(bb[1])` \pm 1.96\times `r nz(ss[1])` = \boldsymbol{[`r nz(lo2[1])`,\ `r nz(hi2[1])`]}$

- 95% CI for $b_1: `r nz(bb[2])` \pm 1.96\times `r nz(ss[2])` = \boldsymbol{[`r nz(lo2[2])`,\ `r nz(hi2[2])`]}$

- 95% CI for $b_2: `r nz(bb[3])` \pm 1.96\times `r nz(ss[3])` = \boldsymbol{[`r nz(lo2[3])`,\ `r nz(hi2[3])`]}$

- 95% CI for $b_3: `r nz(bb[4])` \pm 1.96\times `r nz(ss[4])` = \boldsymbol{[`r nz(lo2[4])`,\ `r nz(hi2[4])`]}$

:::

## Odds CIs

Confidence interval for (population) as odds ratio:

- Lower limit = $\exp(\text{lower limit of } b_1)$

- Upper limit = $\exp(\text{upper limit of } b_1)$

## Classification Accuracy

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true

fitted2 <- fitted(glm2)
class2 <- ifelse(fitted2 > .5, 
                 "pred_yes", "pred_no")
table(class2, Chile$voteYN)
```

```{r}
tab2 <- table(class2, Chile$voteYN)
cor2 <- c(tab2["pred_no", "N"], tab2["pred_yes", "Y"])
acc2 <- sum(cor2) / sum(tab2)
```

$\frac{`r cor2[1]` + `r cor2[2]`}{`r sum(tab2)`} = `r f(100 * acc2)`\%$ accurate, compared with `r f(100 * acc1)`% for the model with only `statusquo` as a predictor

Other considerations

- Is .5 the right cutoff? 
    - What if one category is much less likely than the other?
- This is classifying on the same sample as the one the model was estimated on
    - Cross validation?

:::

## Model Comparison

We can also compare the fit of the two models to determine whether to keep `education` as a predictor

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true

anova(glm1, glm2, test = "LRT")
```

:::

```{r}
a12  <- anova(glm1, glm2, test = "LRT")
chi12 <- a12$Deviance[2]; df12 <- a12$Df[2]; p12 <- a12$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
```

[`anova()` can take two models for comparison]{style="color: #FF7F00;"}

$\chi^2(\text{dif}, `r df12`) = `r f(chi12, 3)`, p `r fp(p12)`$, which `r if (p12 < .05) "indicates significantly better fit in" else "does not indicate significantly better fit for"` the model with both `statusquo` and `education` as predictors over the model with only `statusquo` as a predictor  

## Information Criteria

Another way to compare models is through **information criteria**, which consider the tradeoff between goodness-of-fit (measured by the deviance) and model complexity (measured by a penalty term, usually a function of the number of estimated parameters)

The two most common information criteria: 

- Akaike information criterion (AIC)

- Bayesian information criterion (BIC)

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{AIC} & = \mathsf{Deviance} + \underbrace{2k}_{\text{penalty term}} \\
\mathsf{BIC} & = \mathsf{Deviance} + \underbrace{k\ln(N)}_{\text{penalty term}}
\end{aligned}$$

- $k$: number of estimated parameters; $N$: sample size

- Models with lower AIC or BIC [for the same data]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} are preferred 

## Information Criteria

```{r}
which_lower <- function(v1, v2) {
  if (v2 < v1) "model 2 (`statusquo` + `education` as predictors)" 
  else "model 1 (only `statusquo` as a predictor)"
}
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

AIC is lower for `r which_lower(AIC(glm1), AIC(glm2))`

```{r}
#| echo: true

AIC(glm1); AIC(glm2)
```

BIC is lower for `r which_lower(BIC(glm1), BIC(glm2))`

```{r}
#| echo: true

BIC(glm1); BIC(glm2)
```

I recommend looking at multiple measures (including classification accuracy, likelihood ratio test, information criteria) to decide on the most appropriate model

- Other relevant tools not covered include false positive rates, false negative rates, ROC curves, confusion matrix

:::

## Related Methods


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Methods somewhat similar to logistic regression include: 

- Discriminant function analysis
  
    - Similar goal as logistic regression

    - Find a linear combination of predictors that maximally separates two groups

- Multinomial regression

    - More than 2 ordered categories: proportional odds model

    - More than 2 unordered categories: multinomial logit model
    
- Poisson regression and negative binomial regression

    - Often used for count data

    - Particularly useful for data with excessive 0's (see also zero-inflated models)

:::

## APA Writeup

```{r}
aic <- c(AIC(glm1), AIC(glm2))
bic <- c(BIC(glm1), BIC(glm2))
or_ <- exp(bb); or_lo <- exp(lo2); or_hi <- exp(hi2)   # odds ratios and 95% CIs
lh  <- function(x) if (x < 1) "lower" else "higher"     # direction of an odds ratio

ic_txt <- if (aic[2] < aic[1] & bic[2] < bic[1]) {
  sprintf("Both information criteria also favored the model including education (AIC = %s vs. %s; BIC = %s vs. %s).",
          f(aic[2]), f(aic[1]), f(bic[2]), f(bic[1]))
} else if (aic[2] >= aic[1] & bic[2] >= bic[1]) {
  sprintf("However, both information criteria favored the simpler model with status quo support alone (AIC = %s vs. %s; BIC = %s vs. %s).",
          f(aic[1]), f(aic[2]), f(bic[1]), f(bic[2]))
} else {
  sprintf("Information criteria were mixed: AIC favored the model including education (%s vs. %s), whereas BIC, which penalizes additional parameters more heavily, favored the model with status quo support alone (%s vs. %s).",
          f(aic[2]), f(aic[1]), f(bic[1]), f(bic[2]))
}
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

We fit a logistic regression predicting a "yes" vote (vs. "no") in the 1988 Chilean plebiscite from support for the status quo and education level, with primary school education as the reference group ($N = `r format(nrow(Chile), big.mark = ",")`$). A likelihood ratio test indicated that adding education to a model containing only status quo support `r if (p12 < .05) "significantly improved" else "did not significantly improve"` model fit, $\chi^2(`r df12`) = `r f(chi12)`$, $p `r fp(p12)`$. `r ic_txt`

In the model with both predictors, each one-standard-deviation increase in status quo support was associated with `r f(or_[2])` times the odds of voting "yes," $OR = `r f(or_[2])`$, 95% CI $[`r f(or_lo[2])`, `r f(or_hi[2])`]$, holding education constant. Compared with respondents with a primary school education, respondents with a post-secondary education had `r lh(or_[3])` odds of voting "yes," $OR = `r f(or_[3])`$, 95% CI $[`r f(or_lo[3])`, `r f(or_hi[3])`]$, as did respondents with a secondary education, $OR = `r f(or_[4])`$, 95% CI $[`r f(or_lo[4])`, `r f(or_hi[4])`]$. The model correctly classified `r f(100 * acc2, 1)`% of respondents.

:::
